checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Make a new level and choose Empty Level. Then place a Directional Light and a Sky Atmosphere from the Place Actors panel.
Select the Directional Light and enable Atmosphere Sun Light in its Details panel. This tells the sky to use this light as the sun. Check that Atmosphere Sun Light Index is 0.
Hold Right Ctrl + L and move the mouse to rotate the sun. Find a low sun angle that looks like a sunset, and a high sun angle that looks like noon.
On the Directional Light, turn on Use Temperature. Try a Temperature of 6500 K and then 3000 K, and note how the color of the light changes.

Turn on the Shadow Frustums view: in the viewport, open Show, then Advanced, and enable Shadow Frustums. Look at the rays of the light and notice that they are parallel, which is how sunlight behaves.
Select the Sky Atmosphere and change Mie Scattering Scale up and down. Then set Mie Anisotropy to 0 and to 0.9 and watch the glow around the sun. Reset the values to their defaults when you are done.
Add a second Directional Light and set its Atmosphere Sun Light Index to 1. Make it dim and blue so it works as a moon, and rotate it so it points the opposite way to the sun.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. In a new level, build a small dark room from cubes with a floor and 3 walls, and put a few props inside, such as spheres and cylinders. Set the Directional Light and the Sky Light to a very low brightness, or delete them, so the room is dark.
Place a Point Light. Change Attenuation Radius, which is how far the light reaches, until the light stops at the walls. Then set Source Radius to 20 and look at the highlight on a smooth prop.
Place a Spot Light and aim it at the floor. Set Inner Cone Angle to 20 and Outer Cone Angle to 40. Then try 35 and 40, and compare how soft the edge of the light is.
Place a Rect Light that acts as a TV screen. Set Source Width to 100 and Source Height to 60. Rotate it so its X axis points into the room, because a Rect Light only shines along its X axis.
On the Rect Light, try Barn Door Angle and Barn Door Length. Barn doors are flaps at the sides of the light, and you can use them to cut the light that spills onto the wall.
Set the Mobility of the Rect Light to Movable, and then to Stationary. Note how the shape of the shadow changes between blocky and soft.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a small test level that has a floor and a few props, for example a new Basic level with a few cubes. Place five Point Lights close together so that the areas they light overlap.
Set all five lights to Stationary. Look at the light icons in the viewport and find the one that shows a red X.
Open View Mode, then Optimization Viewmodes, then click Stationary Light Overlap. Take a screenshot that shows the red overlap.
Change one light to Movable and one light to Static. Then check the overlap view again and see what changed.
Select a Movable Point Light and turn Cast Shadows off and then on again. Read the section of the documentation that explains why Movable lights without shadows are cheap.
For each of your five lights, write down which Mobility you would use in a real scene and why. One line for each light is enough.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open Project Settings, then Engine, then Rendering. Confirm that Dynamic Global Illumination Method and Reflection Method are both set to Lumen. Note whether Generate Mesh Distance Fields is turned on.
In a new level, build a small room from cubes with one open door and a bright white floor. Place a strong Directional Light outside so that light bounces into the room through the door.
Add a Post Process Volume and enable Infinite Extent (Unbound), so that its settings apply to the whole level.
In the Post Process Volume, under Global Illumination, try Final Gather Quality at 1 and then at 4. Compare the noise in the dark corners of the room.
Set Max Trace Distance to a very small value, for example 200, and watch what happens in the corners. Then set it back to its old value.

Place a sphere that works like a mirror, with a material that has Roughness 0 and Metallic 1. Under Reflections, set Max Reflection Bounces to 1 and then to 3. Compare the black areas in the reflection.
Try Skylight Leaking at 0 and then at 0.2. Note which value stops the room from becoming fully black.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template, and work in a level with a floor. Open Project Settings, then Engine, then Rendering, and find the Shadows section. Confirm that Shadow Map Method is set to Virtual Shadow Maps.

Place a tall thin mesh, such as a cylinder scaled into a pole, on the floor. Add a Directional Light with Mobility set to Movable, or use the one in the level, and rotate it to a low angle so the shadow is long.
On the Directional Light, set Source Angle to 0.5 and then to 3. Watch the shadow: it should be sharp at the base of the pole and softer far away from it.
Place a Movable Point Light near a prop. Change Source Radius from 0 to 10 and compare the penumbra, which is the soft edge of the shadow.

Open Show, then Visualize, then Virtual Shadow Map, and pick the Cached Page view. Move the camera and watch the green and red pages. Green pages are reused from the frame before, and red pages had to be drawn again.

Add a mesh whose material uses World Position Offset, which moves the surface of the mesh, as wind does on foliage. To make one, create a material, multiply a Sine of a Time node by a small vector such as 0, 0, 20, connect it to World Position Offset, and apply it to a sphere. See how this mesh keeps showing red pages.
On the Directional Light, compare Contact Shadow Length at 0 and at 0.1. Decide if it adds anything to the picture when Virtual Shadow Maps are on.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template, and work in a level with a floor. Create a material named M_LF_Caustic. Open it, and in the Details panel set Material Domain to Light Function.

Add a tiling noise texture or caustic texture, and make it move with a Panner node. Any tiling grayscale texture works, for example a noise or cloud texture from the engine content or the Starter Content. Connect the result to Emissive Color. Keep the values between 0 and 1.
Place a Spot Light with Mobility set to Movable and aim it at a floor. In the Details panel of the light, assign M_LF_Caustic to Light Function Material.
Change the X and Y values of Light Function Scale until the size of the pattern looks right. Also note what the Z value does.

Set Fade Distance so that the pattern fades out far from the camera. Then set Disabled Brightness to the average brightness of your pattern, so the light does not jump in brightness when the pattern fades.
Place an Exponential Height Fog, enable Volumetric Fog on it, and see the pattern appear in the fog.
Open the console and run ShowFlag.VisualizeLightFunctionAtlas 1. Check if your material appears in the atlas, which is one shared texture where Unreal stores light functions.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open an outdoor level that has some difference in height, such as a hill or a Landscape. The level of the template works, or you can make a new level with a sculpted Landscape. Open Place Actors, then Visual Effects, and place an Exponential Height Fog if the level has none.
Move the fog actor up and down on the Z axis and watch where the thick fog sits. Then set Fog Height Falloff to a smaller value and to a larger value and compare.
Set Fog Inscattering Color and Directional Inscattering Color to two clearly different colors. Look toward the sun, and then look away from it, to see where each color is used.
Open Second Fog Data, which is a second layer of fog. Give this layer a small density and a Fog Height Offset so that it sits in a valley.
Set Start Distance to 0 and then to 5000, and compare how the scene looks. Read the Performance section of the documentation to learn why a larger start distance is cheaper.

Do this step if your project uses Sky Atmosphere. Turn on Support Sky Atmosphere Affecting Height Fog in Project Settings, set both inscattering colors to black, and try Height Fog Contribution on the Sky Atmosphere.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Make a new Empty Level with a floor. Place a Directional Light and a Sky Atmosphere, and enable Atmosphere Sun Light on the Directional Light so that the sky uses it as the sun. If you already have a level with this sun and sky, you can use it. Place a Sky Light and set its Mobility to Movable.
Place a chrome sphere, which is a sphere with a material that has Roughness 0 and Metallic 1. You will use it to see the reflection of the sky.
Rotate the sun to a sunset. Notice that the sphere and the lighting on the ground do not change until you press Recapture in the Details panel of the Sky Light.
Enable Real Time Capture on the Sky Light. Rotate the sun again and watch the reflection and the lighting follow it.
Change Cubemap Resolution from 128 to 64, and then to 256. Compare the reflection on the sphere each time.
Open the Advanced section and enable Lower Hemisphere is Solid Color. Note what changes under overhangs, which are places that are covered from above.

Switch Source Type to SLS Specified Cubemap and pick any HDRI, which is a picture of a full sky. The engine content has HDRI cubemaps: turn on Show Engine Content in the settings of the asset picker to find one. Then switch back to SLS Captured Scene.

EAQ44.brief: A prop is a small object in a level, such as a crate or a lamp. Most props are made in another 3D program and brought into Unreal as an FBX file, a common file format for 3D models. The pivot is the point the prop moves and rotates around, and together with the scale it decides how easy the prop is to place later. In this quest you make a simple prop, import it with the correct pivot and size, and check it next to an object of a known size.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Make a small prop such as a crate, a barrel or a lamp in a 3D app such as Blender, which is free. Put it at the origin, which is the zero point of the scene, so that the origin is at one corner or at the bottom center of the prop. If you have no 3D app, build the prop in Modeling Mode in Unreal, then right-click the new Static Mesh, choose Asset Actions, then Export, and save it as an FBX file.
If you use a 3D app, triangulate the mesh before you export it, which means turning all its faces into triangles. Then export it as FBX. Unreal uses the version FBX 2020.2.

In Unreal, click Add/Import in the Content Browser and choose your FBX file. The import window opens. In current versions it is named Interchange Pipeline Configuration, and older versions show a window named FBX Import Options. Before you click Import, look at three settings: the uniform scale (Offset Uniform Scale in the new window, Import Uniform Scale in the old one), Convert Scene Unit, and Generate Lightmap UVs.
Name the asset SM_<PropName>, with the name of your prop in place of <PropName>. Open it in the Static Mesh Editor and check its size and its pivot.
If the scale is wrong, import the file again with a different uniform scale. Do not fix it by scaling the actor in the level.
Place SM_<PropName> in a level next to the default mannequin, which is 180 cm tall, or next to a 100 cm cube, to check its size.

quiz.q: Where does Unreal put the pivot of an imported FBX mesh?
choices: At the origin (0,0,0) of the 3D app scene
At the center of the mesh bounds
At the first vertex of the mesh
At the camera position when you export
quiz.explain: The pivot is always at the origin when exporting. So you should model at the origin, usually with the origin at one corner, to snap well to the grid.

quiz.q: Which is the BEST way to make sure your mesh is triangulated, according to Epic?
choices: Let the importer triangulate it
Let the FBX exporter triangulate it
Triangulate it yourself in the 3D app, controlling the edges
Do nothing, Unreal renders quads directly
quiz.explain: Manual triangulation in the 3D app gives control over edge direction and placement. Automatic triangulation can give bad results.

quiz.q: You want a doorway prop with a hole the player can walk through. What should the collision mesh in the FBX be called if the render mesh is Door_01?
choices: COL_Door_01
UCX_Door_01
Door_01_Collision
PHYS_Door_01
quiz.explain: Custom collision is found by name. UCX_[RenderMeshName] makes a convex collision piece, and you can add _00, _01 for more pieces.

quiz.q: Your FBX has three separate props. What does the importer do by default?
choices: It refuses to import more than one mesh
It always merges them into one Static Mesh
It imports only the first mesh
It makes three separate Static Mesh assets
quiz.explain: Multiple Static Meshes in one FBX become multiple assets unless you turn on the option that combines them at import. It is named Combine Static Meshes in the current import window and Combine Meshes in the older one.

quiz.q: Your prop arrives 100 times too small because the 3D app used meters. Which import option is made for this?
choices: Bake Pivot in Vertex
Remove Degenerates
Convert Scene Unit
Force Front XAxis
quiz.explain: Convert Scene Unit converts the FBX units of measurement to Unreal's unit, centimeters. The uniform scale option of the import window (Offset Uniform Scale, or Import Uniform Scale in the older window) is another way to fix scale.

quiz.q: What does the Generate Lightmap UVs import option do?
choices: It makes a set of unique, non-overlapping UVs for static lighting
It deletes the texture UVs
It makes the mesh use Nanite
It bakes the lighting into vertex colors
quiz.explain: Generate Lightmap UVs creates a unique, non-overlapping UV set that baked (static) lighting can use.

checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a simple prop in the Static Mesh Editor. You can use SM_Door from the Props folder of the Starter Content, or your own mesh with a name that starts with SM_.
In the Collision menu, add a Box Simplified Collision. Then add a Sphere Simplified Collision and see that both shapes now exist. Use Remove Collision to delete them.
Open a prop with a more complex shape, for example SM_Chair from the Starter Content. Try 10-DOP, 18-DOP and 26-DOP from the Collision menu and look at how the shapes differ.
Try Auto Convex Collision, which builds the collision from several simple shapes called hulls. Change Hull Count and Max Hull Verts, click Apply, and compare the result.
Build a collision by hand. Add a Box Simplified Collision, then move and scale it to fit one part of the prop. Duplicate it with Ctrl + D and fit the copies to the other parts.
Place the prop in a level, set Simulate Physics to true, and press Play. Then change the Collision Preset and see what changes.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template, and open any level. Press SHIFT+5 to enter Modeling Mode. If Modeling Mode is missing, enable the plugin named Modeling Tools Editor Mode first.
In the Create category, place a Box with Output Type set to Static Mesh. This is the body of your prop. Then place a Cylinder that cuts into the Box.
Select the Box first, and then the Cylinder. Open Model, then Boolean, and use Difference A - B to cut a hole in the Box. Click Accept.
Select the result and open Model, then PolyGroup Edit. Select the top face and use Extrude to add a lip. Then select the outer edges and use Bevel. Click Accept.
Open Xform, then Edit Pivot, and set the pivot to Bottom. Click Accept.
Save the asset as SM_Quick_<Name>, with a name of your choice in place of <Name>. Place two copies of it in the level.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. You need a mesh made in Modeling Mode, with UVs that are not clean yet. If you have none, enter Modeling Mode, create a Box as a Static Mesh, and cut a hole into it with a Cylinder and the Boolean tool. Right-click the mesh in the Content Browser and open the UV Editor.
In Display, turn on a checker texture as the background. Look at the 3D Viewport and find places where the checker squares are stretched.
Run AutoUV with the default method, Patch Builder, and click Apply. Then look at the checker squares again.
Use the Seam tool to cut one seam on an edge that players will not see. A seam is a cut that lets the surface unfold flat. Then use Unwrap on that island, which is one connected piece of the UV map.
Use Layout with the type Repack so that no islands overlap inside the 0-1 square. Click Apply and then Save.
In the level, assign a material with a visible texture to the mesh. Compare how it looks now with how it looked before.
